claim: NG2 cells receive a major synaptic input from interneurons in the developing neocortex.
source: NG2 cells, oligodendrocyte progenitors, receive a major synaptic input from interneurons in the developing neocortex.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: NG2 cells form a transient and structured synaptic network with interneurons in the developing somatosensory cortex.
source: We show that NG2 cells of the developing somatosensory cortex form a transient and structured synaptic network with interneurons that follows its own rules of connectivity.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental approaches throughout the manuscript.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons are highly connected to NG2 cells.
source: Fast-spiking interneurons, highly connected to NG2 cells, target proximal subcellular domains containing GABAA receptors with γ2 subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by paired recording data showing higher connection probability for FSIs compared to NFSIs.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons target proximal subcellular domains of NG2 cells containing GABAA receptors with γ2 subunits.
source: Fast-spiking interneurons, highly connected to NG2 cells, target proximal subcellular domains containing GABAA receptors with γ2 subunits.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing VGAT+/PV+ puncta distribution and pharmacological experiments with diazepam.

claim: Non-fast-spiking interneurons are poorly connected with NG2 cells.
source: Conversely, non-fast-spiking interneurons, poorly connected with these progenitors, target distal sites lacking this subunit.
evidence: This is supported by paired recording data showing lower connection probability for NFSIs.

claim: Non-fast-spiking interneurons target distal sites of NG2 cells lacking γ2 subunits.
source: Conversely, non-fast-spiking interneurons, poorly connected with these progenitors, target distal sites lacking this subunit.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry showing VGAT+/PV− puncta distribution and lack of diazepam effect on NFSI-NG2 cell connections.

claim: Interneuron-NG2 cell connectivity maps exhibit a local spatial arrangement reflecting innervation only by the nearest interneurons.
source: In the network, interneuron-NG2 cell connectivity maps exhibit a local spatial arrangement reflecting innervation only by the nearest interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by holographic photolysis mapping data showing connections never exceeding 70 µm intersomatic distance.

claim: The interneuron-NG2 cell microcircuit architecture shows a connectivity peak at PN10.
source: This microcircuit architecture shows a connectivity peak at PN10, coinciding with a switch to massive oligodendrocyte differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by paired recording data showing connection probability across different postnatal days.

claim: The connectivity peak at PN10 coincides with a switch to massive oligodendrocyte differentiation.
source: This microcircuit architecture shows a connectivity peak at PN10, coinciding with a switch to massive oligodendrocyte differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data showing increased CC1+/Olig2+ cell density from PN11.

claim: GABAergic innervation of NG2 cells is temporally and spatially regulated from the subcellular to the network level in coordination with the onset of oligodendrogenesis.
source: Hence, GABAergic innervation of NG2 cells is temporally and spatially regulated from the subcellular to the network level in coordination with the onset of oligodendrogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: NG2-expressing cells are the progenitors of myelinating oligodendrocytes.
source: The discovery of bona fide synapses formed on non-neuronal NG2-expressing cells (Bergles et al., 2000), the progenitors of myelinating oligodendrocytes, has challenged the dogma that synapses are a unique feature of neurons in the central nervous system.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Bergles et al., 2000.

claim: Functional synapses between neurons and NG2 cells exist throughout the brain.
source: Since then, the existence of functional synapses between neurons and NG2 cells is recognized as a major physiological feature of these cells throughout the brain (Maldonado and Angulo, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Maldonado and Angulo, 2014.

claim: In the somatosensory cortex, NG2 cells receive a major synaptic input from local GABAergic interneurons that disappears after the second postnatal week.
source: In the somatosensory cortex, NG2 cells receive a major synaptic input from local GABAergic interneurons that disappears after the second postnatal (PN) week (Vélez-Fort et al., 2010; Balia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to previous work.

claim: Cortical NG2 cells are transiently embedded in GABAergic microcircuits at a period known to undergo oligodendrocyte differentiation in the neocortex.
source: Cortical NG2 cells are, therefore, believed to be transiently embedded in GABAergic microcircuits at a period known to undergo oligodendrocyte differentiation in the neocortex (Baracskay et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from previous findings with citation to Baracskay et al., 2002.

claim: The connectivity patterns between neocortical interneurons and their neuronal partners are beginning to be elucidated.
source: However, while the connectivity patterns between neocortical interneurons and their neuronal partners begin to be elucidated (Fino and Yuste, 2011; Pfeffer et al., 2013), the rules governing the GABAergic innervation of NG2 cells in the network are elusive.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge with citations.

claim: The rules governing the GABAergic innervation of NG2 cells in the network are elusive.
source: However, while the connectivity patterns between neocortical interneurons and their neuronal partners begin to be elucidated (Fino and Yuste, 2011; Pfeffer et al., 2013), the rules governing the GABAergic innervation of NG2 cells in the network are elusive.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Cortical GABAergic interneurons are one of the most heterogeneous populations of neurons in the brain.
source: Cortical GABAergic interneurons are one of the most heterogeneous populations of neurons in the brain (Cauli et al., 1997; Petilla Interneuron Nomenclature Group et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The diversity of interneurons impacts synaptic signaling and computational capacities of neuronal networks.
source: Their diversity has been a matter of intense investigation for several decades and is known to impact synaptic signaling and computational capacities of neuronal networks (Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008; Fishell and Rudy, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Different types of interneurons target specific subcellular compartments of their postsynaptic neuron.
source: Different types of interneurons target specific subcellular compartments of their postsynaptic neuron.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Subcellular compartmentalization creates a specific distribution of channels, receptors, and signaling mechanisms and allows for effective regulation of synaptic integration, plasticity, and spiking.
source: Such compartmentalization creates a specific distribution of channels, receptors, and signaling mechanisms and allows for an effective regulation of synaptic integration, plasticity, and spiking (Huang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: In neocortical pyramidal neurons, presynaptic parvalbumin-positive, fast-spiking cells innervate proximal postsynaptic sites with GABAARs-containing α1 subunits.
source: For instance, it has been observed that the localization of different GABAA receptors (GABAARs) in neocortical pyramidal neurons is input-specific since presynaptic parvalbumin (PV)-positive, fast-spiking cells innervate proximal postsynaptic sites with GABAARs-containing α1 subunits, whereas bitufted interneurons contact postsynaptic sites with GABAARs-containing α5 subunits (Ali and Thomson, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Ali and Thomson, 2008.

claim: Bitufted interneurons contact postsynaptic sites with GABAARs-containing α5 subunits in neocortical pyramidal neurons.
source: For instance, it has been observed that the localization of different GABAA receptors (GABAARs) in neocortical pyramidal neurons is input-specific since presynaptic parvalbumin (PV)-positive, fast-spiking cells innervate proximal postsynaptic sites with GABAARs-containing α1 subunits, whereas bitufted interneurons contact postsynaptic sites with GABAARs-containing α5 subunits (Ali and Thomson, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Ali and Thomson, 2008.

claim: PV-positive interneurons strongly inhibit one another but provide little inhibition to other subtypes of interneurons.
source: PV-positive interneurons strongly inhibit one another but provide little inhibition to other subtypes of interneurons, whereas somatostatin-positive interneurons strongly inhibit all other interneurons but are poorly interconnected with each other (Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claim: Somatostatin-positive interneurons strongly inhibit all other interneurons but are poorly interconnected with each other.
source: PV-positive interneurons strongly inhibit one another but provide little inhibition to other subtypes of interneurons, whereas somatostatin-positive interneurons strongly inhibit all other interneurons but are poorly interconnected with each other (Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claim: Interneurons carve out unspecific and dense connections with pyramidal cells.
source: Despite the existence of specific connectivity patterns among interneurons, this heterogeneous cell population carves out unspecific and dense connections with pyramidal cells (Fino and Yuste, 2011; Packer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Fino and Yuste, 2011 and Packer et al., 2014.

claim: In 38 out of 147 pairs, action currents elicited in presynaptic interneurons induced inward postsynaptic currents sensitive to the GABAAR antagonist SR95531 in NG2 cells.
source: In 38 out of 147 pairs, action currents elicited in presynaptic interneurons induced inward postsynaptic currents (PSCs) sensitive to the GABAAR antagonist SR95531 in NG2 cells recorded with a CsCl-based intracellular solution (Figure 1A—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from paired recordings.

claim: All unitary interneuron-NG2 cell connections displayed currents with small amplitudes and showed paired-pulse depression without recovery within 250 ms.
source: All unitary connections displayed currents with small amplitudes and showed paired-pulse depression without recovery within 250 ms (Figure 1A—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data characterizing the synaptic properties.

claim: FSIs and NFSIs can be distinguished by their firing properties even if they have not attained maturity at the developmental stage studied.
source: FSIs and NFSIs can be distinguished by their firing properties even if they have not attained maturity at this developmental stage (Daw et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Daw et al., 2007.

claim: FSIs were primarily distinguished from NFSIs by their narrow action potential waveforms with profound after-hyperpolarizations, a negligible spike broadening and spike amplitude reduction during trains.
source: FSIs were primarily distinguished from NFSIs by their narrow action potential waveforms with profound after-hyperpolarizations (AHPs), a negligible spike broadening and spike amplitude reduction during trains (Figure 1B,D,E) (Cauli et al., 1997; Daw et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological parameters with citations to previous work.

claim: Seven other electrophysiological parameters were statistically different between FSIs and NFSIs and clearly separated these neurons in two distinct groups.
source: Other seven parameters were also statistically different between FSIs and NFSIs and clearly separated these neurons in two distinct groups (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data presented in Table 1.

claim: The identity of FSIs was confirmed by the expression of PV in biocytin-labeled interneurons.
source: The identity of FSIs was further confirmed by the expression of PV in biocytin-labeled interneurons, a reliable marker for this cell class that was absent in NFSIs (Figure 1C—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data.

claim: PV was absent in NFSIs.
source: The identity of FSIs was further confirmed by the expression of PV in biocytin-labeled interneurons, a reliable marker for this cell class that was absent in NFSIs (Figure 1C—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data.

claim: FSIs appeared as a relatively homogeneous population with restricted distributions of the main discriminative parameters.
source: As expected for these two classes of interneurons, FSIs appeared as a relatively homogeneous population with restricted distributions of the main discriminative parameters, whereas NFSIs encompassed different subtypes as revealed by the large distribution of their electrophysiological values (Figure 1E—figure supplement 3A) (Cauli et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological parameter distributions with citation.

claim: NFSIs encompassed different subtypes as revealed by the large distribution of their electrophysiological values.
source: As expected for these two classes of interneurons, FSIs appeared as a relatively homogeneous population with restricted distributions of the main discriminative parameters, whereas NFSIs encompassed different subtypes as revealed by the large distribution of their electrophysiological values (Figure 1E—figure supplement 3A) (Cauli et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological parameter distributions with citation.

claim: The proportion of connected FSIs was high compared to the FSI abundance in tested pairs.
source: However, the proportion of connected FSIs was high compared to the FSI abundance in tested pairs (Figure 1G) or within the population of tested FSIs (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is based on analysis of paired recording data shown in Figure 1G and 1H.

claim: The proportion of connected NFSIs was low compared to the NFSI abundance in tested pairs.
source: Conversely, the proportion of connected NFSIs was low compared to the NFSI abundance in tested pairs (Figure 1G) or within the population of tested NFSIs (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is based on analysis of paired recording data shown in Figure 1G and 1H.

claim: The connection probability for FSIs is 0.43.
source: To determine whether differences in the connection probabilities for FSIs (p = 0.43) and NFSIs (p = 0.21) did not arise by chance, we modeled each of the two data sets as observations from two binomial distributions.
evidence: This is calculated from paired recording data.

claim: The connection probability for NFSIs is 0.21.
source: To determine whether differences in the connection probabilities for FSIs (p = 0.43) and NFSIs (p = 0.21) did not arise by chance, we modeled each of the two data sets as observations from two binomial distributions.
evidence: This is calculated from paired recording data.

claim: FSIs and NFSIs have different connection probabilities (p < 0.01).
source: No overlap was observed between these two intervals, indicating that FSIs and NFSIs have different connection probabilities (p < 0.01).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis using binomial distributions and chi-square test.

claim: No significant differences of main discriminative electrophysiological parameters were found between tested and connected NFSIs.
source: In another hand, it is noteworthy that no significant differences of main discriminative electrophysiological parameters were found between tested and connected NFSIs, indicating that NFSIs innervating NG2 cells constitute a heterogeneous population of interneurons as observed in the tested population (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of electrophysiological parameters.

claim: NFSIs innervating NG2 cells constitute a heterogeneous population of interneurons.
source: In another hand, it is noteworthy that no significant differences of main discriminative electrophysiological parameters were found between tested and connected NFSIs, indicating that NFSIs innervating NG2 cells constitute a heterogeneous population of interneurons as observed in the tested population (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of difference in electrophysiological parameters between tested and connected NFSIs.

claim: NFSIs are by far more abundant and diverse but poorly connected to NG2 cells, whereas FSIs are less abundant but highly connected to NG2 cells in the developing GABAergic network.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that NFSIs are by far more abundant and diverse but poorly connected to NG2 cells, whereas FSIs are less abundant but highly connected to NG2 cells in the developing GABAergic network.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the paired recording and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: A transient peak of connectivity occurred at PN10-11 for both FSI and NFSI.
source: Figure 1I illustrates the connection probability of these interneurons at three different postnatal stages. A transient peak of connectivity occurred at PN10-11 for both FSI and NFSI (Figure 1I), indicating that the connectivity of these two classes of interneurons is not differently affected by the stage of development.
evidence: This is based on paired recording data across different postnatal stages shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The connectivity of FSIs and NFSIs is not differently affected by the stage of development.
source: A transient peak of connectivity occurred at PN10-11 for both FSI and NFSI (Figure 1I), indicating that the connectivity of these two classes of interneurons is not differently affected by the stage of development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both FSIs and NFSIs show a peak at PN10-11.

claim: Paired-pulse ratios, PSC1 and PSC2 amplitudes with or without failures, coefficients of variation, and probabilities of response were not significantly different between FSI-NG2 cell and NFSI-NG2 cell connections.
source: Paired-pulse ratios, PSC1 and PSC2 amplitudes with or without failures, coefficients of variation, and probabilities of response were not significantly different between FSI-NG2 cell and NFSI-NG2 cell connections, suggesting that presynaptic mechanisms of GABA release did not participate in the selectivity for presynaptic inputs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of synaptic properties from paired recordings.

claim: Presynaptic mechanisms of GABA release did not participate in the selectivity for presynaptic inputs.
source: Paired-pulse ratios, PSC1 and PSC2 amplitudes with or without failures, coefficients of variation, and probabilities of response were not significantly different between FSI-NG2 cell and NFSI-NG2 cell connections, suggesting that presynaptic mechanisms of GABA release did not participate in the selectivity for presynaptic inputs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of differences in presynaptic parameters.

claim: Rise and decay times are faster for unitary FSI-NG2 cell connections compared to NFSI-NG2 cell connections.
source: However, we observed a significant difference in current kinetics with rise and decay times faster for unitary FSI-NG2 cell connections (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of current kinetics from paired recordings shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: No correlation was observed for rise and decay times with respect to the postnatal day for either FSI-NG2 cell or NFSI-NG2 cell connections.
source: It is noteworthy that no correlation was observed for rise and decay times with respect to the postnatal day for either FSI-NG2 cell or NFSI-NG2 cell connections (p > 0.05).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of current kinetics across postnatal days.

claim: VGAT+/PV+ puncta were more abundant than VGAT+/PV− on the soma of NG2 cells.
source: VGAT+/PV+ puncta were more abundant than VGAT+/PV− on the soma, whereas their proportion was relatively similar in NG2 cell branches (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is based on quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The proportion of VGAT+/PV+ and VGAT+/PV− puncta was relatively similar in NG2 cell branches.
source: VGAT+/PV+ puncta were more abundant than VGAT+/PV− on the soma, whereas their proportion was relatively similar in NG2 cell branches (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is based on quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The distribution of puncta was significantly closer to the soma for VGAT+/PV+ than for VGAT+/PV− puncta.
source: Furthermore, the distribution of puncta was significantly closer to the soma for VGAT+/PV+ than for VGAT+/PV− puncta (Figure 2E) with a mean distance in branches of 12.8 ± 1.2 µm and 22.5 ± 1.3 µm, respectively (p < 0.0001 excluding puncta on the soma).
evidence: This is based on quantification of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: VGAT+/PV+ puncta were homogeneously distributed in the space at the vicinity of analyzed NG2 cells.
source: VGAT+/PV+ puncta were homogeneously distributed in the space at the vicinity of analyzed NG2 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is based on spatial analysis of puncta distribution shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: FSIs contact preferentially NG2 cell somata and proximal branches, whereas NFSIs mainly contact distal branches.
source: These results indicate that FSIs contact preferentially NG2 cell somata and proximal branches, whereas NFSIs mainly contact distal branches.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunohistochemistry data showing differential distribution of VGAT+/PV+ and VGAT+/PV− puncta.

claim: The differential distribution of presynaptic inputs on NG2 cells is consistent with the faster current kinetics observed for unitary FSI-NG2 cell connections.
source: This is consistent with the faster current kinetics observed for unitary FSI-NG2 cell connections and demonstrates a differential distribution of presynaptic inputs on NG2 cells, according to the interneuron identity.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the anatomical and electrophysiological findings.

claim: Around 40% of cortical NG2 cells express mRNAs for the GABAARs containing γ2 subunits in the second PN week.
source: We recently showed that GABAARs of NG2 cells in the second PN week had a variable and complex subunit composition with around 40% of cortical NG2 cells expressing mRNAs for the GABAARs containing γ2 subunits (Balia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work by Balia et al., 2015.

claim: The effect of diazepam on extracellularly evoked currents in NG2 cells is very variable.
source: In agreement with transcript expression, the effect of the positive modulator diazepam (DZP; a benzodiazepine acting on receptors containing the γ2 subunit) on extracellularly evoked currents is also very variable (Passlick et al., 2013; Balia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Numerous VGAT+/γ2+ and VGAT+/γ2− puncta are present on NG2+ cell membranes of the soma and branches at PN10.
source: We observed numerous VGAT+/γ2+ and VGAT+/γ2− puncta on NG2+ cell membranes of the soma and branches as previously observed for PV/VGAT+ in biocytin-loaded cells.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: VGAT+/γ2+ synaptic puncta on neurons can be clearly distinguished from those present on NG2 cells at PN10.
source: In addition, VGAT+/γ2+ synaptic puncta on neurons can be clearly distinguished from those present on NG2 cells at this developmental stage (Figure 3A), corroborating the presence of VGAT+ puncta on these progenitors.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Diazepam significantly increased the amplitude of unitary synaptic currents in connected FSI-NG2 cell pairs without modifying the paired-pulse ratio.
source: This benzodiazepine significantly increased the amplitude of unitary synaptic currents in connected FSI-NG2 cell pairs without modifying the paired-pulse ratio (PPR), whereas it did not affect currents of unitary NFSI-NG2 cell connections (Figure 3B–C; PPR of 0.55 ± 0.08 and 0.38 ± 0.05 with and without DZP for FSIs and 0.46 ± 0.13 and 0.54 ± 0.14 with and without DZP for NFSIs, respectively, p > 0.05).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments during paired recordings shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Diazepam did not affect currents of unitary NFSI-NG2 cell connections.
source: This benzodiazepine significantly increased the amplitude of unitary synaptic currents in connected FSI-NG2 cell pairs without modifying the paired-pulse ratio (PPR), whereas it did not affect currents of unitary NFSI-NG2 cell connections (Figure 3B–C; PPR of 0.55 ± 0.08 and 0.38 ± 0.05 with and without DZP for FSIs and 0.46 ± 0.13 and 0.54 ± 0.14 with and without DZP for NFSIs, respectively, p > 0.05).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments during paired recordings shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: FSIs preferentially targeted proximal postsynaptic sites of NG2 cells containing GABAARs with γ2 subunits.
source: Hence, FSIs preferentially targeted proximal postsynaptic sites of NG2 cells containing GABAARs with γ2 subunits, whereas NFSIs favored more distal sites lacking this subunit.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of anatomical, kinetic, and pharmacological data.

claim: NFSIs favored more distal sites lacking γ2 subunits.
source: Hence, FSIs preferentially targeted proximal postsynaptic sites of NG2 cells containing GABAARs with γ2 subunits, whereas NFSIs favored more distal sites lacking this subunit.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of anatomical, kinetic, and pharmacological data.

claim: A highly specific spatial arrangement of synaptic inputs exists at the subcellular level in NG2 cells.
source: Overall, the analyses of current kinetics, 3D reconstructions of PV/VGAT+ puncta, and pharmacology of γ2-containing GABAARs demonstrated that FSIs and NFSIs target distinct subcellular segregated domains of NG2 cells, containing different GABAARs. A highly specific spatial arrangement of synaptic inputs, thus, exists at the subcellular level in NG2 cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Extracellular stimulation of neuronal fibers induces postsynaptic currents in NG2 cells that can reach hundreds of pA in the somatosensory cortex.
source: The extracellular stimulation of neuronal fibers induces postsynaptic currents in NG2 cells that can reach hundreds of pA in the somatosensory cortex (Maldonado et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Current amplitudes of unitary interneuron-NG2 cell connections are very small compared to extracellularly evoked currents.
source: However, current amplitudes of unitary interneuron-NG2 cell connections are very small compared to extracellularly evoked currents, suggesting that a single NG2 cell is densely connected by many interneurons in the network, but that a single interneuron contacts a glial progenitor through a restricted number of release sites.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of unitary and extracellularly evoked current amplitudes.

claim: A single NG2 cell is densely connected by many interneurons in the network.
source: However, current amplitudes of unitary interneuron-NG2 cell connections are very small compared to extracellularly evoked currents, suggesting that a single NG2 cell is densely connected by many interneurons in the network, but that a single interneuron contacts a glial progenitor through a restricted number of release sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the small amplitude of unitary connections compared to extracellularly evoked currents.

claim: A single interneuron contacts a glial progenitor through a restricted number of release sites.
source: However, current amplitudes of unitary interneuron-NG2 cell connections are very small compared to extracellularly evoked currents, suggesting that a single NG2 cell is densely connected by many interneurons in the network, but that a single interneuron contacts a glial progenitor through a restricted number of release sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the small amplitude of unitary connections and confirmed by quantal analysis.

claim: In 8 out of 18 connections, quantal analysis revealed no statistical differences between cumulative distributions of PSC1 and PSC2 amplitudes, excluding failures.
source: In 8 out of 18 connections, quantal analysis revealed no statistical differences between cumulative distributions of PSC1 and PSC2 amplitudes, excluding failures, although the response probabilities were significantly higher for PSC1 (Figure 4A,B,E,F; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on quantal analysis of paired recording data shown in Figure 4.

claim: PSCs in 8 out of 18 connections result from the release of only one quantum of transmitters.
source: This implies that PSCs result from the release of only one quantum of transmitters, and therefore, a single vesicle was released per connection (Stevens and Wang, 1995).
evidence: This is inferred from quantal analysis with citation to Stevens and Wang, 1995.

claim: The mean quantal size is −7.71 ± 0.71 pA in the recording conditions used.
source: The mean amplitude of PSCs without failures corresponded to a mean quantal size of −7.71 ± 0.71 pA in our recording conditions.
evidence: This is calculated from paired recording data.

claim: Some interneurons innervate NG2 cells probably through one release site, independent of the presynaptic interneuron identity and the postnatal day.
source: These interneurons, thus, innervate NG2 cells probably through one release site, independent of the presynaptic interneuron identity and the postnatal day (5 FSIs and 3 NFSIs displayed single vesicular release at postnatal days from PN8 to PN13).
evidence: This is inferred from quantal analysis data.

claim: For 10 out of 18 pairs, quantal analysis showed statistical differences between cumulative amplitude distributions and response probabilities of PSC1 and PSC2, indicating that more than one vesicle were released per connection.
source: For the other 10 pairs, quantal analysis showed statistical differences between cumulative amplitude distributions and response probabilities of PSC1 and PSC2, indicating that more than one vesicle were released per connection (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This is based on quantal analysis of paired recording data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Connections with double vesicular release probably displayed double release sites.
source: Thereby, these connections exhibited double vesicular release and probably displayed double release sites.
evidence: This is inferred from quantal analysis showing amplitudes and probabilities around twice for PSC1.

claim: Interneurons established a point-to-point communication with NG2 cells through single- or double-release sites.
source: In addition to the specific spatial distribution of GABAergic inputs impinging on NG2 cells, interneurons established a point-to-point communication with these progenitors through single- or double-release sites.
evidence: This is a summary of the quantal analysis findings.

claim: The restricted innervation of NG2 cells by interneurons contrasts with the ability of interneurons to innervate other neurons through multiple release sites at the same PN stage.
source: This restricted innervation contrasts with the ability of interneurons to innervate other neurons through multiple release sites at the same PN stage (Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011.

claim: MNI-glutamate has a blocking effect on GABAARs in brain slices.
source: However, as many other cages, it has a blocking effect on GABAARs in brain slices (Fino et al., 2009) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Fino et al., 2009 and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A concentration of 50 µM MNI-glutamate has minimal effect on GABAARs of NG2 cells while triggering efficiently action potentials in interneurons at a single-cell resolution.
source: We found that a concentration of 50 µM MNI-glutamate fulfilled these two prerequisites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental testing shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The amplitudes of PSCs induced in NG2 cells by photostimulation were smaller than those in pyramidal neurons.
source: As expected for connections with a limited number of release sites, the amplitudes of PSCs induced in NG2 cells by photostimulation were smaller than those in pyramidal neurons (Figures 5A,C, 6B–E).
evidence: This is based on holographic photolysis mapping data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The probability to find a connected pair was lower for NG2 cells than for pyramidal neurons.
source: Either in the sample of tested cells (Figure 5G) or in maps showing at least one connection (Figure 5H), the probability to find a connected pair was lower for NG2 cells than for pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is based on holographic photolysis mapping data shown in Figure 5G,H.

claim: Connectivity maps of NG2 cells involved very local microcircuits with connections at interneuron-NG2 cell intersomatic distances never exceeding 70 µm.
source: Interestingly, connectivity maps of NG2 cells involved very local microcircuits with connections at interneuron-NG2 cell intersomatic distances never exceeding 70 µm and cumulative distributions of intersomatic distances significantly different for connected and unconnected interneurons (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is based on holographic photolysis mapping data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The connection probability highly decreased after intersomatic distances of 50 µm for NG2 cells.
source: Moreover, the connection probability highly decreased after intersomatic distances of 50 µm (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is based on holographic photolysis mapping data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Connectivity maps of pyramidal cells were relatively homogeneous within 100 μm with similar cumulative distributions of intersomatic distances between connected and unconnected cells.
source: On the contrary, connectivity maps of pyramidal cells were relatively homogeneous within 100 μm with similar cumulative distributions of intersomatic distances between connected and unconnected cells in agreement with previous reports (Fino and Yuste, 2011) (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is based on holographic photolysis mapping data shown in Figure 6H with citation to previous work.

claim: The local architecture of interneuron-NG2 cell connections did not result from the impossibility to detect connections over 70 µm with holographic photolysis.
source: The local architecture of interneuron-NG2 cell connections, thus, did not result from the impossibility to detect connections over 70 µm with holographic photolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with pyramidal cell connectivity maps which show connections beyond 70 µm.

claim: Interneuron-NG2 cell microcircuits are arranged according to a specific connectivity pattern that follows a very local microarchitecture.
source: These findings reveal that interneuron-NG2 cell microcircuits are arranged according to a specific connectivity pattern that follows a very local microarchitecture.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the holographic photolysis mapping data.

claim: The production of premyelinating oligodendrocyte in the cerebral cortex starts during the first postnatal week and reaches a peak at PN14 when compared to PN21.
source: Indeed, the production of premyelinating oligodendrocyte in the cerebral cortex starts during the first postnatal week and reaches a peak at PN14 when compared to PN21 (Trapp et al., 1997; Baracskay et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The connection probability reached a peak at PN10, when 44% of pairs were connected, and then decreased.
source: We observed that the connection probability reached a peak at PN10, when we found 44% of connected pairs, and then decreased (Figure 7A), confirming the transient GABAergic innervation of NG2 cells (Vélez-Fort et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on paired recording data across postnatal days shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The time course of connectivity is specific for NG2 cells since the probability of interneuron-to-neuron connection is known to increase with postnatal cortical development.
source: This time course of the connectivity is specific for NG2 cells since the probability of interneuron-to-neuron connection is known to increase with postnatal cortical development (Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The density of CC1+/Olig2+ cells was low at PN9 and PN10 and significantly increased from PN11.
source: The density of CC1+/Olig2+ cells was low at PN9 and PN10 and significantly increased from PN11 (Figure 7A–F).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A-F.

claim: The peak of synaptic connectivity of cortical NG2 cells at PN10 coincides with a switch to a massive NG2 cell differentiation occurring between PN10 and PN11 in cortical layer V.
source: Therefore, the peak of synaptic connectivity of cortical NG2 cells at PN10 coincides with a switch to a massive NG2 cell differentiation occurring between PN10 and PN11 in cortical layer V (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on the combined analysis of connectivity and differentiation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous synaptic activity increases from PN8 to PN10 and then decreases at PN13.
source: As expected from paired recordings and previous studies (Vélez-Fort et al., 2010; Balia et al., 2015), the frequency of spontaneous synaptic activity increases from PN8 to PN10 and then decreases at PN13 (0.12 ± 0.02 Hz, 0.24 ± 0.05 Hz, 0.12 ± 0.02 Hz, respectively; p < 0.05 for PN10).
evidence: This is based on analysis of spontaneous synaptic activity with citations to previous work.

claim: No statistical differences were observed on the averaged amplitudes of spontaneous synaptic currents between PN8, PN10, and PN13.
source: However, no statistical differences were observed either on the averaged amplitudes of spontaneous synaptic currents or Na+ current densities between PN8, PN10, and PN13 (amplitude of synaptic currents: −10.45 ± 1.04 pA, −12.75 ± 1.27 pA, −12.07 ± 0.90 pA, respectively; Na+ current densities: 22.59 ± 2.99 pA/pF, 23.46 ± 3.56 pA/pF, 26.10 ± 3.72 pA/pF, respectively; p > 0.05).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: No statistical differences were observed on Na+ current densities between PN8, PN10, and PN13.
source: However, no statistical differences were observed either on the averaged amplitudes of spontaneous synaptic currents or Na+ current densities between PN8, PN10, and PN13 (amplitude of synaptic currents: −10.45 ± 1.04 pA, −12.75 ± 1.27 pA, −12.07 ± 0.90 pA, respectively; Na+ current densities: 22.59 ± 2.99 pA/pF, 23.46 ± 3.56 pA/pF, 26.10 ± 3.72 pA/pF, respectively; p > 0.05).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: No correlation was observed between the Na+ current density and the frequency of spontaneous synaptic events at PN8 and PN13 when connectivity is low.
source: Interestingly, while no correlation was observed between the Na+ current density and the frequency of spontaneous synaptic events at PN8 and PN13 when connectivity is low, a positive correlation was observed at PN10 when connectivity is high and the switch to differentiation starts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A positive correlation was observed between Na+ current density and frequency of spontaneous synaptic events at PN10 when connectivity is high and the switch to differentiation starts.
source: Interestingly, while no correlation was observed between the Na+ current density and the frequency of spontaneous synaptic events at PN8 and PN13 when connectivity is low, a positive correlation was observed at PN10 when connectivity is high and the switch to differentiation starts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Interneurons build up a large number of functional synapses in more immature NG2 cells at the onset of massive oligodendrocyte differentiation (PN10) and then GABAergic synapses disassemble.
source: These data suggest that interneurons build up a large number of functional synapses in more immature NG2 cells at the onset of massive oligodendrocyte differentiation (PN10) and then, GABAergic synapses disassemble.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between Na+ current density and synaptic frequency at PN10.

claim: The transient NG2 cell-synaptic connectivity is spatially and temporally regulated in coordination with the active differentiation phase of these progenitors in the second PN week.
source: The transient NG2 cell-synaptic connectivity is thus not only spatially, but also temporally regulated in coordination with the active differentiation phase of these progenitors in the second PN week.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the temporal analysis of connectivity and differentiation.

claim: NG2 cells form a transient and highly organized network with interneurons that is characterized by a high-connection probability at PN10, a specific distribution of synaptic inputs on cell bodies and branches, a restricted number of contacts per interneuron, and very local connectivity maps.
source: We demonstrate that NG2 cells form a transient and highly organized network with interneurons that is characterized by a high-connection probability at PN10, a specific distribution of synaptic inputs on cell bodies and branches, a restricted number of contacts per interneuron, and very local connectivity maps.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: GABAergic innervation of NG2 cells appears as a finely regulated process that follows its own logic, which cannot be inferred from previous studies on NG2 cells and on classical neuronal synapses.
source: GABAergic innervation of NG2 cells, thus, appears as a finely regulated process that follows its own logic, which cannot be inferred from previous studies on NG2 cells and on classical neuronal synapses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion emphasizing the novelty of the findings.

claim: In the neocortex, different classes of interneurons, guided by genetically determined mechanisms, target distinct subcellular domains of pyramidal neurons, allowing a differential compartmentalized signal processing.
source: In the neocortex, different classes of interneurons, guided by genetically determined mechanisms, are known to target distinct subcellular domains of pyramidal neurons, allowing a differential compartmentalized signal processing (Huang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Input-specific projections exist for interneuron-NG2 cell connections.
source: We demonstrate that input-specific projections also exist for interneuron-NG2 cell connections.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: NG2 cells compartmentalize FSI- and NFSI-input regions as revealed by distinct anatomical locations of PV+ and PV− contacts and by a different distribution of GABAARs with or without γ2 subunits at postsynaptic sites.
source: NG2 cells compartmentalize FSI- and NFSI-input regions as revealed by distinct anatomical locations of PV+ and PV− contacts and by a different distribution of GABAARs with or without γ2 subunits at postsynaptic sites.
evidence: This is a summary of the anatomical and pharmacological findings.

claim: FSIs and NFSIs impinging on NG2 cells probably encode distinct information that regulates different cellular NG2 cell processes.
source: FSIs and NFSIs impinging on these glial progenitors, thus, probably encode distinct information that regulates different cellular NG2 cell processes.
evidence: This is speculative inference based on the differential targeting of FSIs and NFSIs.

claim: FSI synapses located at proximal sites and somata could regulate NG2 cell differentiation by controlling gene expression.
source: Located at proximal sites and somata, FSI synapses could regulate NG2 cell differentiation by controlling gene expression, whereas distal NFSI synapses could affect motility or migration.
evidence: This is speculative inference based on the subcellular location of synapses.

claim: Distal NFSI synapses could affect motility or migration of NG2 cells.
source: Located at proximal sites and somata, FSI synapses could regulate NG2 cell differentiation by controlling gene expression, whereas distal NFSI synapses could affect motility or migration.
evidence: This is speculative inference based on the subcellular location of synapses.

claim: GABA probably promotes NG2 cell migration through the activation of GABAA receptors.
source: Indeed, it has been suggested that GABA probably promotes NG2 cell migration through the activation of GABAA receptors (Tong et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Tong et al., 2009.

claim: FSIs play a major role in controlling NG2 cell activity during early stages of postnatal development.
source: NG2 cells receive inputs from both FSIs and NFSIs, but FSIs are proportionally more connected to these progenitors, suggesting that they play a major role in controlling NG2 cell activity during early stages of postnatal development.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher connection probability of FSIs.

claim: Immature FSIs possess different electrophysiological properties compared to adult animals, such as high-input resistance, relatively low-membrane time constants, and a certain degree of spike-frequency adaptation.
source: Compared to adult animals, immature FSIs possess different electrophysiological properties, such as high-input resistance, relatively low-membrane time constants, and a certain degree of spike-frequency adaptation, and are thus unlikely to perform the same function that in mature circuits (Okaty et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Okaty et al., 2009.

claim: Immature FSIs are unlikely to perform the same function as in mature circuits.
source: Compared to adult animals, immature FSIs possess different electrophysiological properties, such as high-input resistance, relatively low-membrane time constants, and a certain degree of spike-frequency adaptation, and are thus unlikely to perform the same function that in mature circuits (Okaty et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the different electrophysiological properties with citation.

claim: FSIs probably do not contribute to coordinating cortical neuronal activity in the perinatal period since FSI-pyramidal cell connections are detected only from PN5.
source: In fact, FSIs probably do not contribute to coordinating cortical neuronal activity in the perinatal period since FSI-pyramidal cell connections are detected only from PN5 (Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011.

claim: FSIs start to influence cortical activity only during the second postnatal week.
source: FSIs start to influence cortical activity only during the second postnatal week (Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011), and as shown here, it is also at this period that they constitute a significant, transient presynaptic input to NG2 cells.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011.

claim: Synaptic communication between FSIs and NG2 cells could play a role in the maturation of FSIs in the developing neuronal network.
source: Synaptic communication between FSIs and NG2 cells could, therefore, play a role in the maturation of FSIs in the developing neuronal network.
evidence: This is speculative inference based on the temporal coincidence of FSI-NG2 cell connectivity and FSI maturation.

claim: Local cortical interneurons are believed to lack myelin because they possess relatively short axons that do not project outside the cortex.
source: Although local cortical interneurons are believed to lack myelin because they possess relatively short axons that do not project outside the cortex, Somogyi et al. (1983) demonstrated the presence of myelin enwrapping the axon of basket cells, most probably FSIs, in cats (Somogyi et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated as general belief with citation to Somogyi et al., 1983 showing an exception.

claim: Somogyi et al. demonstrated the presence of myelin enwrapping the axon of basket cells, most probably FSIs, in cats.
source: Although local cortical interneurons are believed to lack myelin because they possess relatively short axons that do not project outside the cortex, Somogyi et al. (1983) demonstrated the presence of myelin enwrapping the axon of basket cells, most probably FSIs, in cats (Somogyi et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Somogyi et al., 1983.

claim: Myelination is an activity-dependent process.
source: Since myelination is an activity-dependent process (Zalc and Fields, 2000), an interesting possibility would be that the restricted point-to-point GABA release at unitary interneuron-NG2 cell connections encodes a signal that triggers NG2 cell differentiation and myelination of the presynaptic interneuronal axon, preferentially that of FSIs.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Zalc and Fields, 2000.

claim: The restricted point-to-point GABA release at unitary interneuron-NG2 cell connections could encode a signal that triggers NG2 cell differentiation and myelination of the presynaptic interneuronal axon, preferentially that of FSIs.
source: Since myelination is an activity-dependent process (Zalc and Fields, 2000), an interesting possibility would be that the restricted point-to-point GABA release at unitary interneuron-NG2 cell connections encodes a signal that triggers NG2 cell differentiation and myelination of the presynaptic interneuronal axon, preferentially that of FSIs.
evidence: This is speculative inference based on the findings and known activity-dependent myelination.

claim: Myelination of neocortical FSIs is likely to occur since myelin is important for the organization of Kv1 channels.
source: Myelination of neocortical FSIs is likely to occur since myelin is important for the organization of Kv1 channels (Rasband et al., 1998), and these channels have been proposed to mediate the variability in FSI-firing patterns (Golomb et al., 2007).
evidence: This is speculative inference with citations to support the reasoning.

claim: Kv1 channels have been proposed to mediate the variability in FSI-firing patterns.
source: Myelination of neocortical FSIs is likely to occur since myelin is important for the organization of Kv1 channels (Rasband et al., 1998), and these channels have been proposed to mediate the variability in FSI-firing patterns (Golomb et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Golomb et al., 2007.

claim: Axonal signals are essential to regulate oligodendrocyte production and survival.
source: In addition, axonal signals are essential to regulate oligodendrocyte production and survival (Barres et al., 1992; Trapp et al., 1997), and interneuronal axons transiently contact NG2 cells during active-cortical oligodendrogenesis.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Barres et al., 1992 and Trapp et al., 1997.

claim: Interneuronal axons transiently contact NG2 cells during active-cortical oligodendrogenesis.
source: In addition, axonal signals are essential to regulate oligodendrocyte production and survival (Barres et al., 1992; Trapp et al., 1997), and interneuronal axons transiently contact NG2 cells during active-cortical oligodendrogenesis.
evidence: This is based on the findings of the study.

claim: One-photon holographic photolysis is a suitable alternative tool to elicit action potentials in neurons at single-cell resolution and find unitary connections.
source: On the contrary, we show that one-photon holographic photolysis is a suitable alternative tool to elicit action potentials in neurons at single-cell resolution and find unitary connections.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion based on the successful application of the technique.

claim: No specificity exists between the spatial profiles of interneuron-pyramidal cell connectivity maps.
source: It has been reported that no specificity exists between the spatial profiles of interneuron-pyramidal cell connectivity maps, and thus, that pyramidal cells do not form specific networks in the neocortex (Fino and Yuste, 2011; Packer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Fino and Yuste, 2011 and Packer et al., 2014.

claim: Pyramidal cells do not form specific networks in the neocortex.
source: It has been reported that no specificity exists between the spatial profiles of interneuron-pyramidal cell connectivity maps, and thus, that pyramidal cells do not form specific networks in the neocortex (Fino and Yuste, 2011; Packer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Fino and Yuste, 2011 and Packer et al., 2014.

claim: Interneuron-NG2 cell connectivity maps follow a local spatial arrangement, reflecting a focal control of NG2 cell activity by interneurons.
source: In contrast, interneuron-NG2 cell connectivity maps follow a local spatial arrangement, reflecting a focal control of NG2 cell activity by interneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the holographic photolysis mapping data.

claim: The local network formed by interneurons and NG2 cells is embedded within the developing neuronal network.
source: The existence of a local network formed by interneurons and NG2 cells, embedded within the developing neuronal network, implies the involvement of selective molecular and cellular mechanisms ensuring this local connectivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings of local connectivity.

claim: Selective molecular and cellular mechanisms ensure the local connectivity between interneurons and NG2 cells.
source: The existence of a local network formed by interneurons and NG2 cells, embedded within the developing neuronal network, implies the involvement of selective molecular and cellular mechanisms ensuring this local connectivity. These mechanisms remain to be elucidated.
evidence: This is speculative inference about mechanisms that would explain the findings.

claim: In the developing postnatal brain, the proper maturation of interneuron–neuron microcircuits requires the interactions between intrinsic genetic programs and neuronal activity.
source: In the developing postnatal brain, the proper maturation of interneuron–neuron microcircuits requires the interactions between intrinsic genetic programs and neuronal activity (Cossart, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Cossart, 2011.

claim: The emergence of properly organized GABAergic neuronal microcircuits is not only confined to neurons, but also includes a non-neuronal cell type.
source: We demonstrate that the emergence of properly organized GABAergic neuronal microcircuits is not only confined to neurons, but also includes a non-neuronal cell type.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: After the peak of synaptic connectivity at PN10, the decrease of GABAergic synaptic innervation of NG2 cells is accompanied by a decrease in the amplitude of GABAAR-mediated miniature events.
source: Interestingly, after the peak of synaptic connectivity at PN10, the decrease of GABAergic synaptic innervation of NG2 cells is accompanied by other relevant physiological changes in these progenitors: (1) there is a decrease in the amplitude of GABAAR-mediated miniature events (Balia et al., 2015); (2) Kir channels start to be upregulated (Kressin et al., 1995); and (3) the first wave of oligodendrocytes arising from Nkx2.1-expressing precursors of MGE and the anterior entopeduncular area is eliminated (Kessaris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Balia et al., 2015.

claim: After the peak of synaptic connectivity at PN10, Kir channels start to be upregulated in NG2 cells.
source: Interestingly, after the peak of synaptic connectivity at PN10, the decrease of GABAergic synaptic innervation of NG2 cells is accompanied by other relevant physiological changes in these progenitors: (1) there is a decrease in the amplitude of GABAAR-mediated miniature events (Balia et al., 2015); (2) Kir channels start to be upregulated (Kressin et al., 1995); and (3) the first wave of oligodendrocytes arising from Nkx2.1-expressing precursors of MGE and the anterior entopeduncular area is eliminated (Kessaris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Kressin et al., 1995.

claim: After the peak of synaptic connectivity at PN10, the first wave of oligodendrocytes arising from Nkx2.1-expressing precursors of MGE and the anterior entopeduncular area is eliminated.
source: Interestingly, after the peak of synaptic connectivity at PN10, the decrease of GABAergic synaptic innervation of NG2 cells is accompanied by other relevant physiological changes in these progenitors: (1) there is a decrease in the amplitude of GABAAR-mediated miniature events (Balia et al., 2015); (2) Kir channels start to be upregulated (Kressin et al., 1995); and (3) the first wave of oligodendrocytes arising from Nkx2.1-expressing precursors of MGE and the anterior entopeduncular area is eliminated (Kessaris et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Kessaris et al., 2006.

claim: The GABAergic synaptic input probably does not control per se cortical oligodendrocyte production, which is a protracted process that occurs during several weeks, even after the loss of functional synapses.
source: The GABAergic synaptic input probably does not control per se cortical oligodendrocyte production, which is a protracted process that occurs during several weeks, even after the loss of functional synapses.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the temporal mismatch between connectivity and the full time course of oligodendrogenesis.

claim: The coincidence between the peak of connectivity (PN10) and the switch to a massive NG2 cell differentiation from PN10 raises the possibility that the interneuron-NG2 cell network sets precisely the onset of oligodendrogenesis occurring in deep layers of the neocortex during the second postnatal week.
source: However, the coincidence between the peak of connectivity (PN10) and the switch to a massive NG2 cell differentiation from PN10 raises the possibility that the interneuron-NG2 cell network sets precisely the onset of oligodendrogenesis occurring in deep layers of the neocortex during the second postnatal week.
evidence: This is speculative inference based on the temporal coincidence of connectivity peak and differentiation switch.

claim: A transient and structured NG2 cell connectivity is necessary to set the onset of oligodendrogenesis.
source: This would explain why a transient and structured NG2 cell connectivity is necessary.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the functional significance of the findings.
